title: Waymo cars stranded on San Francisco streets as Fourth of July gridlock drains batteries

reading.body:
Waymo's autonomous vehicles were not designed to handle the traffic conditions created by Fourth of July celebrations in San Francisco. Multiple vehicles became immobilized when severe gridlock prevented them from reaching charging locations before their batteries depleted. The system operated without sufficient safeguards for predictable but irregular surge events in urban mobility demand.

The incident shows that autonomous vehicle services can fail when deployed in conditions outside their normal operating parameters, even in the cities where they run regularly. One vehicle caught fire after driving over fireworks on the road, an environmental hazard the system did not anticipate. Waymo's response required human intervention to tow the stranded vehicles and remove them from service.

It is not established whether better battery management, dynamic rerouting to avoid congestion, or advance warning systems could have prevented the gridlock from disabling the fleet. The company stated it is evaluating resilience improvements but has not disclosed what specific technical or operational changes will result.

reports.title: Waymo cars stranded on San Francisco streets as Fourth of July gridlock drains batteries

summary:
Multiple Waymo autonomous vehicles became stranded on San Francisco streets on Saturday evening after Fourth of July fireworks celebrations caused severe traffic congestion that drained their batteries. Video footage showed at least a dozen stationary Waymo vehicles, many of them Jaguar I-PACE models, lined up on streets near the Golden Gate Bridge. The company attributed the gridlock to major traffic disruptions, high volumes of travelers, and unplanned road closures. One vehicle caught fire after driving over fireworks set off on the road, though no injuries were reported.

The incident prompted Waymo's roadside assistance team to tow away the vehicles, and the company stated it is evaluating ways to improve resilience during major traffic disruptions. City officials, including Mayor Daniel Lurie's office, acknowledged the delays affecting over 100,000 people in the area and said they plan to discuss the situation with public and private partners to improve future experiences. This is not the first challenge for Waymo in San Francisco, as the company briefly paused service in December after a citywide power outage disabled traffic lights and caused some vehicles to stall.
